messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Nguyen, a 51-year-old South Eastern Asian man, has been experiencing significant distress since his wife’s violent outburst over six months ago. Mr. Nguyen had always trusted her completely, but the event shattered that trust and left him feeling deeply violated. The night of the abuse was vivid in his memory; it began as an ordinary evening at home, but soon escalated into a terrifying ordeal when he found himself facing unpredictable violence from someone he loved. Since then, Mr. Nguyen feels extremely tired most days, both physically and emotionally drained. This exhaustion is often triggered by seemingly minor situations where he feels uncomfortable or unsteady, such as unpredictable work meetings or interactions with colleagues at the office. These triggers frequently lead him to feel as if he were in imminent danger, even when there’s no real threat present. The memory of that night persists in fragments, appearing suddenly and disappearing just as quickly. He often experiences these sudden pieces of the memory during moments of exhaustion or discomfort, reinforcing his sense of vulnerability. The memories also force their way into his mind at unpredictable times, causing him to lose focus on tasks at work and leading to a growing fear that he might be attacked again. Mr. Nguyen has come to believe that nothing good can happen to him anymore, as the experience left him feeling dehumanized and betrayed by someone he trusted deeply. These negative appraisals have created a cycle of distress where his fear of danger is perpetually heightened. For instance, when he feels tired or uncomfortable at work, these feelings quickly escalate into a sense that he must constantly check behind him to ensure no one is following. His job as a tax inspector has become increasingly difficult due to this ongoing vigilance. He frequently finds himself distracted by his constant need to monitor his surroundings and his own state of fatigue. This has led to mistakes at work, which in turn intensify his feelings of dehumanization and betrayal. Mr. Nguyen is certain that he is no longer seen as a competent professional but merely an object subjected to scrutiny. The unpredictable nature of the memories exacerbates these negative appraisals, making him feel like an outsider even in familiar settings. He has started to avoid social gatherings and family events, fearing that any small discomfort or exhaustion might trigger another episode. This avoidance only reinforces his sense of betrayal and the belief that nothing good will ever happen again. Mr. Nguyen’s current state is marked by a pervasive sense of fear and isolation. The combination of feeling unsafe unless he can see all directions around him and constantly looking behind to check for threats has made daily activities unbearable. He finally sought help after realizing how deeply this experience had affected his relationship with his wife, as well as his ability to function at work. What frightens Mr. Nguyen most is the possibility that he will never feel safe again and that others might view him merely as a victim rather than a capable individual. His greatest hope is to regain a sense of normalcy and control over his life, free from the constant fear and unpredictability that now dominate his days.
